title: Chikungunya Virus Infection
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Chikungunya is an Aedes‑mosquito transmitted alphavirus causing acute febrile illness with severe polyarthralgia. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and early PCR; management is supportive with NSAIDs after the acute phase.

sections.p: Chikungunya is an arthropod‑borne alphavirus endemic in East Africa, the Indian Ocean islands and increasingly in low‑resource urban settings. Outbreaks follow Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus proliferation after rains.
b: Attack rate can exceed 50 % in naive populations
Case‑fatality <0.1 % but morbidity from chronic arthritis is high

sections.p: A single‑stranded positive‑sense RNA virus, 11 kb genome, enveloped, belonging to the Togaviridae family. Replicates in the cytoplasm of endothelial and fibroblast cells, causing a vigorous inflammatory response.
b: No animal reservoir; humans are the primary source
Mutations in the E1 gene increase replication in Aedes albopictus

sections.p: Transmitted by the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes; virus replicates in the mosquito midgut and salivary glands, allowing transmission during subsequent feeds. Vertical (transovarial) transmission is rare but documented.
b: Peak biting at dawn and dusk
Breeds in clean, stagnant water containers

sections.p: Acute febrile polyarthritis. Illness progresses through three phases: acute (days 1‑7), sub‑acute (weeks), and chronic (months‑years). Severe joint pain may mimic rheumatoid arthritis.
b: Fever, severe myalgia, rash (maculopapular, often trunk‑limited)
Symmetrical polyarthralgia, especially ankles, wrists, fingers

sections.p: Clinical suspicion in a febrile patient with severe polyarthralgia during an outbreak. Laboratory confirmation is essential when resources allow.

t.b: Detects viral RNA; positive confirms infection early
Shows recent infection; IgM persists 2‑3 months

sections.p: No specific antiviral; care is symptomatic and preventive.
b: Acetaminophen for fever; avoid NSAIDs until dengue excluded
NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) after dengue ruled out for joint pain
Vector control: eliminate standing water, use insecticide‑treated nets

sections.p: Key points examiners love: differentiate from dengue, recognize chronic arthritis, know why NSAIDs are delayed, and understand vector control measures.
b: Severe joint pain out of proportion to fever points to chikungunya
Rash in chikungunya is usually non‑purpuric, unlike dengue’s petechiae
Chronic arthritis may require DMARD referral

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dehydration or inability to take oral fluids
Signs of severe dengue (hemorrhage, plasma leakage) suggesting co‑infection

faq.q: How to distinguish chikungunya from dengue at the bedside?
faq.a: Chikungunya has markedly severe symmetric joint pain and a non‑purpuric rash; dengue more often shows high fever, retro‑orbital pain, and a petechial rash.

faq.q: When can NSAIDs be safely started?
faq.a: Only after dengue is excluded (negative rapid test or platelet count >100 ×10⁹/L) because NSAIDs increase bleeding risk.

faq.q: What is the risk of chronic arthritis?
faq.a: Up to 40 % of adults develop persistent joint pain lasting months; early physiotherapy improves outcomes.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with 3‑day fever, severe ankle pain and a maculopapular rash during a local outbreak – what is your next diagnostic step? — Order RT‑PCR if within 5 days; otherwise obtain IgM ELISA.
Why must you withhold ibuprofen until dengue is ruled out? — NSAIDs impair platelet function and increase bleeding risk in dengue, which can coexist in the same vector environment.
A patient has chronic symmetric polyarthritis 6 months after acute illness – how do you manage? — Refer for physiotherapy and consider DMARDs if functional impairment persists.
What vector control measures are most effective in low‑resource settings? — Source reduction of water containers, community education, and use of insecticide‑treated nets.
How does chikungunya cause joint pain at the cellular level? — Viral replication in synovial fibroblasts triggers cytokine release (IL‑6, TNF‑α) leading to inflammatory arthritis.

A child presents with fever, rash, and thrombocytopenia – how do you differentiate dengue from chikungunya? — Check platelet count; <100 ×10⁹/L favors dengue, while normal platelets with severe arthralgia favor chikungunya.
What are the indications for hospital admission? — Persistent high fever, dehydration, severe pain limiting oral intake, or neurological complications.
Explain why RT‑PCR loses sensitivity after day 7. — Viremia declines sharply after the first week; antibodies dominate, making nucleic‑acid detection less reliable.
